statements.quote: In a preregistered online experiment, we assigned occupation-specific, incentivized writing tasks to 453 college-educated professionals, and randomly exposed half of them to ChatGPT.
statements.locator: Saved author manuscript p. 1, Abstract; markdown line 15

statements.quote: In a preregistered online experiment, we recruited 453 experienced, college-educated professionals on the survey platform Prolific and assigned each to complete two occupation-specific, incentivized writing tasks (21).

The tasks, which included writing press releases, short reports, analysis plans, and delicate emails, comprised 20-to 30-minute assignments designed to resemble real tasks performed in these occupations; indeed, most of our participants reported completing similar tasks before and rated the assigned tasks as realistic representations of their everyday work (see Supplementary Materials).

In addition to output quality evaluations, we collected self-reported and objective measures of participants’ time spent on the tasks and took snapshots of participants’ outputs each minute while they performed the task, to construct objective measures of activity and detect ChatGPT usage (see Supplementary Materials).

A complete description of our experimental design, copies of relevant survey questionnaires, and additional figures validating our central measures and extending our main results are included in the Supplementary Materials.
statements.locator: p. 3, Method, final paragraph; markdown line 83

statements.quote: Descriptive statistics about the sample, as well as balance and selective attrition tests, are available in Table 1.
statements.locator: p. 3, Method, final paragraph; markdown line 83

statements.quote: Our partly within-person design, which controls for performance on the pre-treatment task, should eliminate any influence of selective attrition on our results; in the Supplementary Materials, we also report Lee bounds (24) on our main results and versions of our results controlling for employment status and occupation, which confirm that our results are highly robust to selective attrition.
statements.locator: p. 3, Method, final paragraph; markdown line 83

statements.quote: Self-reported and objective measures indicate about 10-20% of the control group used ChatGPT on the tasks (see Supplementary Materials), meaning there was at least a 60-percentage point experimentally-induced gap in usage between our treatment and control groups on the second task.
statements.locator: p. 4, Takeup of ChatGPT, paragraph 2; markdown line 109

statements.quote: Our estimates reflect the effects of ChatGPT on the average productivity of the 60-70% of participants whose usage was determined by their treatment assignment, and constitute lower bounds on the effects of ChatGPT usage on productivity; in the Supplementary Materials, we report two-stage least squares results adjusting our estimates upwards for imperfect compliance.
statements.locator: p. 4, Takeup of ChatGPT, paragraph 2; markdown line 109

statements.quote: Evaluator grades also suggest this editing was ineffectual: there was no correlation between how long a participant was active after pasting in the ChatGPT text and the grade they ultimately received, and treated respondents who used ChatGPT did not receive higher average grades than raw ChatGPT output we gave to evaluators to grade (see Supplementary Materials).
statements.locator: p. 5, Human-Machine Interactions, paragraph 2; markdown line 151

statements.quote: Due to the small sample size in this group, the confidence interval includes zero and the treatment and control group differ in terms of average pre-treatment grades; see Supplementary Materials.

deposits.notes: Primary replication package for the saved manuscript and Science paper. Both the paper/form URL https://osf.io/xd7qw/?view_only=b8dac58dd6f44b979bf81069022fa392 and DOI https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/XD7QW returned HTTP 200; the DOI resolved to this canonical URL. The unauthenticated node API reported public=true and read permission. Root file listing and all folder/pagination requests returned HTTP 200; children API returned HTTP 200 with 0 children. All 26 files are listed, excluding empty folders. The intermediate and output folders are empty, so cleaned analysis datasets and computed results must be regenerated. No license was specified in node metadata, DataCite rightsList, or inspected documentation. All downloaded data were read only in memory. rows_checked=4092 refers to the entire raw/grading_long_complete.csv, whose 4092 rows are unfiltered participant-task-grader records, NOT 4092 people; overall, writing, content and originality each have 3616 nonmissing entries. The entire raw/grading_wide_complete.csv has 2020 rows and pairs A/B scores by participant and grader. The entire raw/grades.csv has 343 grading-survey rows and 277 columns; it holds repeated essay.1A through essay.7B text fields with corresponding prolific_pid.* author IDs and overall*/rating* scores. Thus written outputs, not just grader justifications, are directly confirmed. Texts can be reshaped and deduplicated by author and task; raw ChatGPT benchmarks, test records, and retry submissions need separate handling. The README explains that Prolific IDs were replaced with random hashes and that rating*_1, rating*_2, rating*_3 denote writing, content, originality. raw/fullsurvey.csv is 22753065 bytes: only bytes 0-999999 were requested and received (HTTP 206, Content-Range bytes 0-999999/22753065), yielding 29 complete preview records before an incomplete trailing record. Its total row count was not determined. Its header has 668 columns, including prolific_pid, treatment, a_first, incentive_arm, occupation, task_a, task_b, finished and consent fields. Preview treatment values include 0 and 1; incentive values include linear, convex and exact. These are preview values, not analyzed arm counts. README p. 6 defines treatment 0=control and 1=treatment, and a_first maps occupational tasks A/B to pre/post treatment. Of the preview IDs, 21 matched the complete grading file, with 156 rating rows and 133 nonmissing values for each of the four scores. columns_checked lists selected columns from those directly inspected files. raw/fullsurvey_fulltext.csv is 28066308 bytes and was not downloaded; README pp. 1 and 3 say it preserves complete essays and snapshots because fullsurvey.csv text can be truncated by Stata. Essay text is independently confirmed in the smaller grades.csv. Additional inspected raw files: grading.xlsx 688 rows; grading_retry.xlsx 376 rows; followupsurvey.csv 418 rows; twomonth_followup.csv 377 rows (all HTTP 200; raw rows include incomplete/test entries). The July 21 README instructs changing the master's grade-cleaning call to code/3 - grade cleaning_jul21.do. Code/2 documents consent/completion, duplicate, quality and grader-overlap exclusions; the revised grade-cleaning script additionally excludes retry/test and low-agreement graders. Code/4 lines 104-136 explicitly specifies participant-grader grade-change regressions with grader, occupation-by-task-order and incentive fixed effects and participant-clustered SEs for all, linear/convex and exact-time samples. Code/5 includes separate writing/content/originality analyses. No full replication or final sample-count calculation was performed.

Found through the DataCite first-author search as DOI 10.17605/OSF.IO/Q3GDU, under the earlier title Experimental Evidence on the Productivity Effects of Large Language Models - Data. Node metadata names Noy and Zhang (2023), states IDs are anonymized hashes, and reports public=true. Landing page, node API, file API and children API all returned HTTP 200; 8 files and 0 children; no code files or license specified. This is an earlier deposit of S1, not an additional randomized study; prefer xd7qw for the final paper. rows_checked=3774 refers to the complete grading_long_complete.csv (748578 bytes), which has 3402 nonmissing values for each of overall, writing, content and originality; these are unfiltered rating records, not people. The whole anon_completegrade.csv (16949195 bytes) was read: 484 grading-survey rows, including essay.1A through essay.7B, matching id.*_HASH author-ID fields, PID_HASH grader ID, and the corresponding overall/rating variables. The fullsurvey.csv file is 22034862 bytes; only its first 1000000 bytes were retrieved (HTTP 206, Content-Range bytes 0-999999/22034862), yielding 29 complete preview records and a header with 667 columns, including prolific_pid, treatment, a_first, incentive_arm, task_a and task_b. The preview includes both treatment values and all three incentive groups; it is not an analysis sample and its totals must not be treated as arm Ns. Twenty preview participant IDs matched the complete grade file, producing 144 rating rows with 128 nonmissing values for each of the four scores. The full survey's total row count, exact final-paper sample coverage and equivalence of this older data version to the current package were not established. columns_checked contains selected directly inspected columns from these files.

Public preregistration for S1 under the earlier Large Language Models title. The paper's version DOI https://doi.org/10.1257/rct.10882-2.1 returned HTTP 200 and resolved to https://www.socialscienceregistry.org/trials/10882/history/177681. The one publicly linked analysis-plan document at https://www.socialscienceregistry.org/versions/177680/docs/version/document returned HTTP 200 and was read in memory as DOCX; n_files counts the one visible public attachment, not any hidden materials. The page describes planned randomized conditions and outcomes but posts no person-level observations. Some registry fields have Request Information notices; no request, login or account creation was attempted. Its Data Publication field says public data are not available, but this is contradicted by direct anonymous access to the two OSF deposits. Its final-sample fields list 457 total, 238 control and 219 treatment, which differ from the saved manuscript's recruited/descriptive counts; these are registry entries, not verified randomized or analyzed Ns for the saved PDF. The preregistered design and analysis plan do not establish which final analysis specification was used.

what_we_could_compute: S1-O1 through S1-O5: after reconstructing the retained sample and mapping occupational tasks A/B to pre/post treatment, calculate each person's mean evaluator score and arm-level means, SDs, SEs and complete-case participant Ns, separately for overall, writing, content and originality, with linear/convex and exact-time subgroup results. This addresses the analyzed-count open item and the missing separate-score statistics; the code uses overall grade for the main grade outcome, so do not invent an additional composite or treat S1-O1 and S1-O3 as independent measures.

Using the posted inclusion/exclusion and grade-cleaning code, count unique retained participant IDs by treatment, outcome and incentive subgroup, and reconstruct recorded attrition/exclusions. Raw file row counts and the bounded survey preview are not analyzed Ns. A complete assignment-stage flow and exact number originally randomized still require checking the entire survey and when assignment fields were populated; public documentation alone does not settle that open item.

Re-estimate separate overall/originality/writing/content treatment effects and their SEs or confidence intervals, and reproduce the fixed-15-minute grade contrast. Code/4 identifies the exact-time contrast as participant-grader grade-change regression with participant-clustered SEs. The accessible code addresses specification questions, but does not establish everything printed in the inaccessible Supplementary Materials or recover rubric text absent from the inspected files.

Compare outputs of the all-participant and linear/convex specifications when investigating the manuscript's 0.45-versus-0.41 SD discrepancy. Those specifications are present in the code, but the discrepancy itself has not been explained or resolved by this availability check.

Compute between-person textual diversity or similarity by randomized arm from participant-linked essay text in grades.csv, after deduplicating repeated grader presentations, applying the final sample restrictions, distinguishing occupational task prompts and pre/post timing, and excluding nonparticipant ChatGPT benchmarks and retries. The separately posted fullsurvey_fulltext.csv documents a source of complete essays and minute snapshots; its contents were not inspected because it exceeds 20 MB.
notes: Checked 2026-10-09 with unauthenticated Python urllib requests using User-Agent atlas-screening/0.1.
